items.title: ICT, Digital India & e-Governance Models
items.body:
## In one line
What ICT means, the Digital India programme that drives it, and the simple ways government uses technology to serve citizens.

## The story
**ICT (Information and Communication Technology)** is what you get when **computing** (information technology — computers, data, software) joins with **communication technology** (telephones, the internet, networks). This **convergence of computing and telecommunication** is the defining feature of modern ICT — so ICT is *not* just computer hardware; it includes telecom and the internet. It powers banking, education, health, shopping and farming, and is a key enabler of **e-governance, financial inclusion and digital service delivery**.

To spread ICT, the government launched **Digital India on 1 July 2015** (run by **MeitY**, the IT ministry). It rests on **nine pillars** (such as Broadband Highways, Universal Mobile Connectivity, Public Internet Access, **e-Governance**, **e-Kranti** (electronic delivery of services), Information for All, Electronics Manufacturing, IT for Jobs and Early Harvest) and three visions: infrastructure as a utility, governance and services on demand, and digital empowerment.

Government uses technology in four relationships, called **e-governance models** — just four answers to "who is being served?":
- **G2C** (Government-to-Citizen) — e.g. downloading a certificate on **DigiLocker**.
- **G2B** (Government-to-Business) — e.g. **GeM** / e-procurement for vendors.
- **G2G** (Government-to-Government) — e.g. departments sharing data via **API Setu**.
- **G2E** (Government-to-Employee) — e.g. staff payroll/HR portals.

Delivery platforms you should know: **UMANG** (a single mobile app for multiple government services), **DigiLocker** (cloud storage and issuance of verified digital documents), **e-Sign** (Aadhaar-based online electronic signature) and **API Setu** (open-API exchange enabling system interoperability — the G2G inter-departmental data link).

## Why it matters
The Digital India launch year, the nine pillars (a "which is NOT a pillar" trap), and the four G2x models are near-certain Paper-II facts.

## Picture it

| Model | Who is served | Example |
|---|---|---|
| G2C | Citizen | DigiLocker, UMANG |
| G2B | Business | GeM, e-procurement |
| G2G | Government | API Setu data exchange |
| G2E | Employee | Payroll/HR portals |

## Terms explained
- **MeitY** — Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology.
- **e-Kranti** — the Digital India pillar for electronic delivery of services.
- **DigiLocker** — a government app storing legally valid digital documents.
- **API** — a standard way for software systems to talk to each other.

## Don't confuse
**Green Energy Corridors** is a *power-transmission* scheme (MNRE), **not** a Digital India pillar — a classic distractor.

## Remember it
Models "**C-B-G-E**" = Citizen, Business, Government, Employee — the four "who" of e-governance.

## TL;DR
- ICT = computing + communication technology; it underpins daily life and governance.
- Digital India launched 1 July 2015 (MeitY), on nine pillars; e-Kranti = electronic service delivery.
- e-governance models: G2C, G2B, G2G, G2E.
- Platforms: UMANG (services app), DigiLocker (documents), e-Sign (Aadhaar signature), API Setu (interoperability).
keyPoints: ICT = convergence of information technology (computing) and communication technology (telecom/internet).
Digital India launched 1 July 2015 by MeitY, built on nine pillars.
e-Kranti is the electronic-service-delivery pillar of Digital India.
e-Governance models: G2C (citizen), G2B (business), G2G (government), G2E (employee).
UMANG = unified services app; DigiLocker = verified digital documents; e-Sign = Aadhaar e-signature; API Setu = open-API interoperability.
items.source: MeitY / PIB — Digital India programme & e-Governance models
items.mnemonic: Models 'C-B-G-E' = Citizen, Business, Government, Employee — the four 'who' of e-governance.

items.title: India Stack & Digital Public Infrastructure
items.body:
## In one line
The set of open digital "building blocks" — identity, payments and data — that lets India deliver services to a billion people cheaply and online.

## The story
**India Stack** is India's **Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI)**: a set of **open APIs** (shared software connectors anyone can plug into) built in layers so services can be **presence-less, paperless and cashless**. Think of it as public roads, but for digital services:
- **Identity** — **Aadhaar** gives each person a unique digital ID for instant verification (e-KYC).
- **Payments** — **UPI** moves money between any two bank accounts in real time.
- **Data** — **DigiLocker** stores verified documents; the **Account Aggregator** lets you share financial data only with your consent.
- **Commerce** — **ONDC** is an open network that lets any buyer and seller trade, instead of one company's app.
- **Health** — **CoWIN / ABDM** handled vaccination and digital health records.

**UPI** is the star. Run by **NPCI** (promoted by the RBI) and launched in **2016**, it is the **world's largest real-time retail payment system by volume**; monthly transactions crossed the **16-billion** mark in 2024-25. It is now linked abroad (e.g. Singapore's PayNow) for cheaper remittances.

DPI matters because it slashes the cost of delivering services, widens **financial inclusion**, and makes **Direct Benefit Transfers (DBT)** flow straight to people with less leakage.

## Why it matters
"Who runs UPI", the India Stack layers, and the ONDC "open network, not an app" distinction are repeat exam points.

## Picture it

| Layer | Component | Role |
|---|---|---|
| Identity | Aadhaar | Unique ID / e-KYC |
| Payments | UPI | Real-time money transfer |
| Data | DigiLocker, Account Aggregator | Documents; consent-based sharing |
| Commerce | ONDC | Open e-commerce network |
| Health | CoWIN / ABDM | Vaccination, health records |

## Terms explained
- **API** — a connector letting software systems exchange data in a standard way.
- **NPCI** — National Payments Corporation of India, which operates UPI.
- **Account Aggregator** — a system to share your financial data only with your permission.
- **DBT** — Direct Benefit Transfer: paying subsidies straight into bank accounts.

## Don't confuse
**ONDC is an open network, not a single company's app** — it connects many buyers, sellers and apps, unlike one proprietary platform.

## Remember it
"**Aadhaar knows you, UPI pays, DigiLocker proves, ONDC sells**."

## TL;DR
- India Stack = open-API DPI across identity, payments and data.
- Layers: Aadhaar (ID), UPI (payments), DigiLocker/Account Aggregator (data), ONDC (commerce), CoWIN (health).
- UPI: run by NPCI, launched 2016, world's largest real-time retail payment system; 16 billion+ monthly transactions (2024-25).
- DPI lowers service costs, widens financial inclusion, powers DBT.
keyPoints: India Stack = open-API digital public infrastructure across identity, payments and data.
Layers: Aadhaar (identity), UPI (payments), DigiLocker & Account Aggregator (data), ONDC (commerce), CoWIN (health).
UPI is operated by NPCI, launched 2016, and is the world's largest real-time retail payment system by volume.
Monthly UPI volumes crossed 16 billion transactions in 2024-25.
Account Aggregator enables consent-based sharing of financial data; ONDC is an open e-commerce network, not a single company's app.

items.title: Data Protection & Cyber Law — DPDP Act 2023, Rules 2025 & IT Act 2000
items.body:
## In one line
India's two core digital laws — the new data-protection law (DPDP Act 2023, Rules 2025) that guards your personal data, and the older IT Act 2000 that governs cyber offences.

## The story
After the Supreme Court declared **privacy a fundamental right** in the **Puttaswamy judgment (2017)**, India needed a law to protect personal data. The **Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023** — India's **first dedicated data-protection law**, enacted August 2023 — is the result. Its **DPDP Rules, 2025** (notified on **14 November 2025**) spell out how it works in practice (consent managers, security safeguards, breach notification, and how the Board functions).

It uses simple roles:
- **Data Principal** — you, the individual the data is about.
- **Data Fiduciary** — the organisation that decides why and how your data is processed.
- **Significant Data Fiduciary** — a large/high-risk fiduciary with extra duties.

A **Data Protection Board of India** decides breaches, with penalties **up to ₹250 crore** per instance. You get rights to **access, correct, erase, complain and nominate**; a **child's data (under 18)** needs **verifiable parental consent**.

The older **Information Technology (IT) Act, 2000** is India's **primary cyber law** for e-commerce and cyber crime, substantially **amended in 2008**. Its famous **Section 66A** (punishing "offensive" online messages) was **struck down** by the Supreme Court in **Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015)** for violating free speech. Other key sections: 43A (data-breach compensation), 69 (interception), 70/70A/70B (protected systems, NCIIPC, CERT-In), 79 (intermediary safe harbour).

## Why it matters
The DPDP year, penalty ceiling and Board, the Rules-2025 date, and the 66A/Shreya Singhal fact are all high-frequency exam points.

## Picture it

| Law | Year | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| IT Act | 2000 (amended 2008) | Primary cyber law; e-commerce, offences |
| DPDP Act | 2023 | First data-protection law; Data Protection Board |
| DPDP Rules | 2025 | Operational rules for the Act |

## Terms explained
- **Data Principal / Fiduciary** — the individual / the organisation handling the data.
- **Verifiable parental consent** — proven approval from a parent before processing a child's data.
- **Safe harbour (Sec 79)** — legal protection for intermediaries (platforms) for user content, under conditions.
- **Puttaswamy (2017)** — the judgment that made privacy a fundamental right.

## Don't confuse
The **DPDP Act (2023)** is the parent law; the **DPDP Rules (2025)** are the detailed rules under it. Different years, different instruments.

## Remember it
"**Principal owns, Fiduciary processes**" — you own your data; the organisation merely handles it.

## TL;DR
- DPDP Act 2023 = India's first data-protection law; DPDP Rules notified 2025.
- Data Protection Board of India; penalties up to ₹250 crore; children's data needs parental consent.
- Roles: Data Principal (you), Data Fiduciary, Significant Data Fiduciary.
- IT Act 2000 (amended 2008) is the primary cyber law; Section 66A struck down in Shreya Singhal (2015).
keyPoints: DPDP Act 2023 is India's first dedicated data-protection law; DPDP Rules were notified in 2025.
DPDP establishes the Data Protection Board of India; penalties up to ₹250 crore per instance.
DPDP roles: Data Principal (individual), Data Fiduciary, Significant Data Fiduciary; children's data needs parental consent.
IT Act 2000 is India's primary cyber law, amended in 2008.
Section 66A was struck down by the SC in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015).
items.source: MeitY / PIB — DPDP Act 2023 & Rules 2025; IT Act 2000; Shreya Singhal (2015)
items.mnemonic: DPDP roles = 'Principal owns, Fiduciary processes' — the individual vs the data handler.

items.title: Cyber Security Architecture & Citizen Redress
items.body:
## In one line
The agencies that defend India's cyberspace and the helplines a citizen uses when hit by online fraud.

## The story
As India goes digital, protecting its networks becomes vital. A set of bodies share the job:
- **CERT-In (Indian Computer Emergency Response Team)** — the **national nodal agency** that responds to cyber incidents; under **MeitY**, recognised by **IT Act Section 70B**. Its **2022 directions** require specified incidents to be **reported within 6 hours**, logs kept 180 days, and KYC/data retention by VPN and cloud providers.
- **NCIIPC** — protects **Critical Information Infrastructure (CII)** (power, banking, telecom, transport) under the **NTRO**, via **IT Act Section 70A**.
- **Cyber Swachhta Kendra** — CERT-In's **botnet-cleaning** and malware-analysis centre.
- **I4C (Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre)** — under the **Ministry of Home Affairs**, coordinates cyber-crime response for citizens.

The **National Cyber Security Policy 2013** was India's first such policy, aiming for a secure cyber ecosystem and a skilled workforce.

Common threats to know:

| Threat | What it does |
|---|---|
| Phishing | fraudulent messages tricking users into revealing credentials (passwords, OTPs) |
| Ransomware | malware that encrypts your files and demands payment (a ransom) |
| DDoS (Distributed Denial of Service) | flooding a server with traffic to deny service to real users |
| Man-in-the-middle | secret interception or alteration of communication between two parties |

If a citizen is defrauded: use the **National Cybercrime Reporting Portal (cybercrime.gov.in)**, the **helpline 1930**, and the **CFCFRMS** system, which can **rapidly freeze** fraudulently transferred money.

## Why it matters
CERT-In vs NCIIPC (sections 70B vs 70A), the 6-hour rule, and the 1930/I4C redress chain are frequent Paper-II and Mains facts.

## Picture it

| Body | Role | Anchor |
|---|---|---|
| CERT-In | Cyber incident response | MeitY; Sec 70B |
| NCIIPC | Protects Critical Info Infrastructure | NTRO; Sec 70A |
| Cyber Swachhta Kendra | Botnet cleaning | Under CERT-In |
| I4C | Cyber-crime coordination; 1930, portal | Home Affairs |

## Terms explained
- **Nodal agency** — the lead body coordinating a function nationally.
- **Critical Information Infrastructure (CII)** — systems whose failure would damage national security or the economy.
- **Botnet** — a network of infected computers controlled by an attacker.
- **CFCFRMS** — Citizen Financial Cyber Fraud Reporting and Management System.

## Don't confuse
**CERT-In responds to incidents (Sec 70B); NCIIPC protects critical infrastructure (Sec 70A).** Different jobs, different sections.

## Remember it
"**1930 to freeze the fraud**" — the number to call fast when money is stolen online.

## TL;DR
- CERT-In (MeitY, Sec 70B) = incident response; its 2022 directions mandate 6-hour reporting.
- NCIIPC (NTRO, Sec 70A) protects Critical Information Infrastructure.
- Cyber Swachhta Kendra cleans botnets; National Cyber Security Policy adopted 2013.
- Citizen redress: I4C (MHA), portal cybercrime.gov.in, helpline 1930, CFCFRMS.
- Threats: phishing, ransomware, DDoS, man-in-the-middle.
keyPoints: CERT-In (under MeitY, Sec 70B) is the national cyber-incident response agency; NCIIPC (under NTRO, Sec 70A) protects Critical Information Infrastructure.
CERT-In's 2022 directions mandate reporting specified cyber incidents within 6 hours.
Cyber Swachhta Kendra is CERT-In's botnet-cleaning centre; National Cyber Security Policy was adopted in 2013.
I4C (under MHA) runs the National Cybercrime Reporting Portal (cybercrime.gov.in) and helpline 1930.
CFCFRMS enables rapid reporting to freeze fraudulently transferred money.
Common threats: phishing, ransomware, DDoS and man-in-the-middle attacks.
items.source: CERT-In cyber-security handbook; NCIIPC; I4C / MHA

items.title: Emerging-Tech Missions — AI, 5G/6G, Quantum, Semiconductors, Supercomputing
items.body:
## In one line
The national missions pushing India into frontier technologies — artificial intelligence, fast networks, quantum, chip-making and supercomputers.

## The story
India has launched a cluster of big-ticket technology missions:
- **IndiaAI Mission (approved 2024)** — outlay about **₹10,372 crore** over five years (MeitY). Seven pillars include **Compute Capacity** (GPUs), an Innovation Centre, a **Datasets Platform (AIKosh)**, Application Development, **FutureSkills**, Startup Financing and **Safe & Trusted AI**. On **deepfakes**, MeitY advisories under the IT Rules 2021 push labelling/traceability of AI-made content, while a dedicated AI law is debated.
- **Connectivity** — **5G launched October 2022** and reached all districts within about two years; the **Bharat 6G Vision (2023)** aims to make India a 6G leader (patents, standards) by around 2030.
- **National Quantum Mission (approved 2023, ~₹6,003 crore)** — quantum computing, quantum-secure **communication (QKD)**, sensing and materials.
- **India Semiconductor Mission (₹76,000 crore)** — approved chip units at **Dholera (Gujarat)** — India's first commercial fab (Tata-PSMC), **Sanand (Gujarat)** (Micron and others) and **Jagiroad/Morigaon (Assam)** (Tata OSAT).
- **National Supercomputing Mission (2015, C-DAC)** — the **PARAM** series; the **PARAM Rudra** supercomputers were dedicated to the nation in 2024.

## Why it matters
Mission outlays, launch years and chip-fab locations are exactly the kind of current-tech facts APPSC asks.

## Picture it

| Mission | Year | Headline figure |
|---|---|---|
| IndiaAI | 2024 | ~₹10,372 crore |
| National Quantum Mission | 2023 | ~₹6,003 crore |
| India Semiconductor Mission | — | ₹76,000 crore |
| 5G launch | Oct 2022 | all districts in ~2 yrs |

## Terms explained
- **GPU** — a chip good at the heavy parallel maths that AI needs.
- **QKD** — Quantum Key Distribution, a way to share encryption keys that is secure by physics.
- **Fab** — a semiconductor fabrication plant that makes chips.
- **OSAT / ATMP** — assembly, testing, marking and packaging of chips.

## Don't confuse
The **IndiaAI Mission** (AI compute, GPUs) is different from the **National Supercomputing Mission** (the PARAM supercomputers) and the **National Quantum Mission** (quantum tech) — three separate programmes.

## Remember it
"**AI-5G-Quantum-Chips-Super**" — the five frontier missions, each with its own ministry and money.

## TL;DR
- IndiaAI Mission (2024, ~₹10,372 cr): compute, AIKosh datasets, FutureSkills, Safe & Trusted AI; deepfakes via IT Rules 2021 advisories.
- 5G launched Oct 2022; Bharat 6G Vision (2023) targets 6G leadership by ~2030.
- National Quantum Mission (2023, ~₹6,003 cr) includes quantum-secure communication.
- India Semiconductor Mission (₹76,000 cr): Dholera & Sanand (Gujarat), Jagiroad/Morigaon (Assam).
- National Supercomputing Mission: PARAM Rudra supercomputers dedicated 2024 (C-DAC).
keyPoints: IndiaAI Mission (2024) has ~₹10,372 crore outlay; pillars include compute capacity, AIKosh datasets, FutureSkills and Safe & Trusted AI.
MeitY advisories address deepfakes/AI-generated content under IT Rules 2021, pending dedicated regulation.

National Supercomputing Mission's PARAM Rudra supercomputers were dedicated in 2024 (C-DAC).

items.title: Connectivity Backbone & Andhra Pradesh e-Governance
items.body:
## In one line
The networks that carry digital services to every village, and how Andhra Pradesh became a leader in technology-driven governance.

## The story
Services need a **backbone** to travel on:
- **BharatNet** — optical-fibre broadband to all gram panchayats (the rural fibre backbone).
- **PM-WANI** — public Wi-Fi hotspots for last-mile access.
- **Common Service Centres (CSC)** — village access points that deliver G2C services.
- **MeghRaj (GI Cloud)** — the government's cloud-computing service and empanelled data centres.

**Andhra Pradesh (AP)** is a pioneer in **data-driven governance**:
- **Real Time Governance Society (RTGS)** runs a **Real Time Governance Centre** that pulls together department data for live monitoring of schemes, disaster response and grievances.
- **e-Pragati** is AP's **enterprise-architecture platform** — a single digital backbone linking departmental services.
- **Praja Sadhikara Survey** was a household **socio-economic data-collection** exercise linking citizen data to entitlements.
- **Mana Mitra** is **WhatsApp-based governance**: via a single mobile (WhatsApp) number, citizens get many services and downloadable certificates. It is anchored in the RTGS framework and is a clear example of the **G2C (Government-to-Citizen)** model.
- **AP FiberNet (APSFL)** is the state-government undertaking providing fibre-optic broadband, internet and cable-TV to homes; it aims to extend affordable last-mile broadband connectivity across the state.
- **Amaravati Quantum Valley** (announced 2025) is being developed in Andhra Pradesh as **India's first quantum-computing hub**, intended to attract investment in quantum computing. It is set to host an **IBM Quantum System Two** powered by IBM's **156-qubit 'Heron' processor**, with **TCS** and **L&T** among the industry partners associated with the project.
- **Google's AI data-centre hub at Visakhapatnam** (announced 2025, about **1 GW**, with **Adani** and **Bharti Airtel** as partners) is planned as Google's largest AI hub in India.

AP shows the shift from portal-based to **chat-based, whole-of-government** delivery — raising both access gains and **data-privacy/DPDP-compliance** questions.

## Why it matters
BharatNet/MeghRaj and the AP initiatives (RTGS, e-Pragati, Mana Mitra) are strong AP-angle questions for Paper-II and Mains.

## Picture it

| Initiative | Purpose |
|---|---|
| BharatNet | Fibre broadband to gram panchayats |
| PM-WANI | Public Wi-Fi hotspots |
| CSC | Rural G2C delivery points |
| MeghRaj | Government cloud |
| RTGS (AP) | Real-time scheme monitoring |
| Mana Mitra (AP) | WhatsApp service delivery |

## Terms explained
- **Gram panchayat** — the village-level unit of local government.
- **Enterprise architecture** — a single integrated design linking all of an organisation's systems.
- **Last-mile** — the final stretch of connectivity reaching the actual user.
- **Whole-of-government** — many departments delivering through one unified channel.

## Don't confuse
**RTGS (Real Time Governance Society)** here is AP's governance body — not the RBI's RTGS (Real Time Gross Settlement) banking system. Same letters, different thing.

## Remember it
"**Fibre to the village, WhatsApp to the citizen**" — BharatNet backbone, Mana Mitra front door.

## TL;DR
- Backbone: BharatNet (fibre to panchayats), PM-WANI (public Wi-Fi), CSC (rural delivery), MeghRaj (govt cloud).
- AP RTGS runs a real-time governance centre; e-Pragati integrates departmental services.
- Praja Sadhikara Survey collected household socio-economic data.
- Mana Mitra delivers AP services/certificates via WhatsApp through RTGS; AP FiberNet gives fibre broadband.
keyPoints: BharatNet delivers fibre broadband to gram panchayats; PM-WANI provides public Wi-Fi; CSCs are rural G2C delivery points.
MeghRaj (GI Cloud) is MeitY's government cloud-computing initiative.
AP's Real Time Governance Society (RTGS) runs a real-time centre for scheme monitoring and grievance redress.
e-Pragati is AP's enterprise-architecture platform integrating departmental services.
Praja Sadhikara Survey was a household socio-economic data-collection exercise.
Mana Mitra delivers AP government services and certificates via WhatsApp through RTGS.
Google's ~1 GW AI data-centre hub (with Adani and Airtel) is being built at Visakhapatnam.
items.source: MeitY / DoT — BharatNet, PM-WANI, CSC, MeghRaj; AP Real Time Governance Society; AP IT & e-Governance Dept

items.title: Emerging Digital Technologies — Blockchain, Web 3.0, Cloud & Communication Tech
items.body:
## In one line
Plain-English explanations of the frontier terms the exam loves — blockchain, NFTs, Web 3.0, cloud models and short-range communication tech.

## The story
**Blockchain** is a **distributed, decentralised public ledger** — a record book copied across many computers (nodes). Entries are **immutable** (cannot be secretly changed) and are agreed by **consensus** (such as Proof-of-Work or Proof-of-Stake). No single user controls it, yet everyone can inspect it; on a **permissionless** chain, applications that depend on its basic features can be built without anyone's permission. It is **not only for cryptocurrency** — it also runs **smart contracts** (self-executing code, e.g. on Ethereum), supply-chain tracking and land records.

- **Cryptocurrency** (like Bitcoin) is **fungible** — every unit is interchangeable, so it works as money.
- An **NFT (Non-Fungible Token)** is a **unique cryptographic token** recorded on a blockchain standing for one specific asset — it can enable digital representation of physical assets (art, property) as well as digital ones; being unique, it cannot be traded at equivalency and is **not** used as everyday money.
- **Web 3.0** is a **decentralised web** where users **own their own data** and services are run by users collectively, not by one corporation.

**Cloud computing** rents IT over the internet in three models:
- **IaaS** — raw compute/storage (e.g. AWS EC2).
- **PaaS** — a platform to build and run apps (e.g. Google App Engine).
- **SaaS** — ready-to-use software (e.g. **Gmail, Outlook, Yahoo Mail**); users can often customise the user interface and change some data fields, and can access their data from any device that connects to the internet.

**Communication technologies** worth knowing: **RFID** (radio tags for identification), **NFC** (Near Field Communication — a contactless technology using electromagnetic radio fields; works only within **about 4 cm**, and can use encryption when sensitive information is sent), **WLAN/Bluetooth** (short-range wireless), **Li-Fi/VLC** (wireless; uses **visible light, 375-780 nm** as the medium to transmit high-speed data, several times faster than Wi-Fi, no electromagnetic interference), **VoLTE** (Voice over LTE — voice carried as data on the 4G network) and **Project Loon** (Google's balloon-based internet for remote areas).

On **AI today**: present-state AI can already diagnose diseases from images, convert text to speech, generate stories/songs and optimise industrial energy — but it **cannot** wirelessly transmit electrical energy (that is unrelated to AI).

## Why it matters
These are classic UPSC-style "consider the statements" S&T questions; knowing the precise distinctions (NFT vs crypto, NFC range, SaaS examples) is what the exam tests.

## Picture it

| Cloud model | User gets | Example |
|---|---|---|
| IaaS | Compute/storage/network | AWS EC2 |
| PaaS | Platform to build apps | App Engine |
| SaaS | Ready software | Gmail / Outlook |

## Terms explained
- **Immutable** — cannot be altered once recorded.
- **Consensus** — the agreed method nodes use to validate new entries.
- **Fungible / non-fungible** — interchangeable (money) / unique (NFT).
- **VLC** — Visible Light Communication (Li-Fi).

## Don't confuse
**NFC is not RFID at a distance** — NFC works only within about **4 cm**, whereas RFID can be read from farther away. And an **NFT is unique (not money)**, unlike **fungible cryptocurrency**.

## Remember it
"**Blockchain = shared book no one owns; NFT = one-of-a-kind; Web 3.0 = you own your data**."

## TL;DR
- Blockchain = decentralised, immutable, consensus-validated ledger; permissionless; not only for crypto.
- NFT = unique (non-fungible) token, not a medium of exchange; crypto is fungible.
- Web 3.0 = decentralised web where users own their data.
- Cloud: IaaS (infrastructure), PaaS (platform), SaaS (software, e.g. Gmail/Outlook).
- NFC ~4 cm (can encrypt); Li-Fi uses visible light (375-780 nm), faster than Wi-Fi; VoLTE = voice over 4G; Project Loon = balloon internet.
keyPoints: Blockchain is a decentralised, immutable public ledger validated by consensus; permissionless chains let anyone build apps and it is not limited to cryptocurrency.
NFTs are unique (non-fungible) tokens on a blockchain, unlike fungible cryptocurrency; they are not a medium of exchange.
Web 3.0 = decentralised web where users own their data and services are user-run, not corporation-run.
Cloud models: IaaS (infrastructure), PaaS (platform), SaaS (software, e.g. Gmail/Outlook).
NFC works only within ~4 cm and can use encryption; RFID/WLAN/Bluetooth are short-range technologies.
Li-Fi/VLC uses visible light (375-780 nm), is faster than Wi-Fi and has no EM interference.
VoLTE = Voice over LTE (both 4G); Project Loon = balloon-based wireless internet.
items.source: NITI Aayog/MeitY primers on Blockchain & DPI; NIST cloud definition; UPSC-standard S&T references (verified Sep 2026)

items.title: Communication & Internet Basics, Telecom Law and Netiquette
items.body:
## How the internet and mobile networks work

**In one line:** the internet is a network of networks that began as ARPANET (1969), the World Wide Web runs on top of it (Tim Berners-Lee, 1989), and mobile networks have moved from analogue 1G to data-only 5G — all governed in India by the Telecommunications Act 2023.

**Why it is asked:** "who invented the WWW", "IPv6 address length", "when did the internet come to India", "which Act replaced the Telegraph Act 1885" and "what is netiquette" are common Paper-II and SSC-type items.

**The story**

The internet grew from the US defence network **ARPANET (1969)**. **Tim Berners-Lee** created the **World Wide Web at CERN in 1989** — web pages linked by **HTTP** and found by **URLs**; the **DNS** translates names like gov.in into numeric **IP addresses**. The old **IPv4** uses 32-bit addresses; **IPv6** uses **128-bit** addresses, giving almost unlimited numbers. Public internet came to India through **VSNL on 15 August 1995**. Data travels long distances in **optical fibre** by **total internal reflection** of light.

Mobile generations: **1G** was analogue voice, **2G (GSM)** was digital and brought SMS, **3G** brought mobile internet, **4G LTE** is all-IP broadband (voice carried as data = VoLTE), and **5G** adds very high speed and very low latency (launched in India in October 2022). The **Telecommunications Act, 2023** replaced the **Indian Telegraph Act, 1885**, and **TRAI (1997)** regulates tariffs and quality.

**Netiquette** ("net etiquette") is the code of good behaviour online: be polite, do not type in ALL CAPITALS (it reads as shouting), do not spam, flame or troll, respect others' privacy and copyright, and check facts before forwarding.

### Internet and telecom milestones

| Item | Fact |
|---|---|
| **ARPANET (1969)** | US defence network that grew into the internet |
| **World Wide Web** | created by Tim Berners-Lee at CERN in 1989 |
| **IPv6** | 128-bit internet addresses (IPv4 uses 32-bit) |
| **DNS (Domain Name System)** | translates domain names into numeric IP addresses |
| **HTTPS** | HTTP secured with encryption (TLS) — shown by the padlock in the browser |
| **Public internet in India** | launched by VSNL on 15 August 1995 |
| **Optical fibre** | carries light signals by total internal reflection |
| **2G (GSM)** | first digital mobile generation — brought SMS |
| **4G LTE** | all-IP mobile broadband; voice on it is VoLTE |
| **5G** | very high speed, very low latency, supports massive IoT |
| **Telecommunications Act, 2023** | replaced the Indian Telegraph Act, 1885 |
| **TRAI (1997)** | Telecom Regulatory Authority of India — regulates tariffs and service quality |
| **Sanchar Saathi (DoT, 2023)** | portal and app to block lost phones (CEIR) and check mobile connections in your name |
| **Satellite broadband (GMPCS)** | internet from low-Earth-orbit satellites; spectrum assigned administratively under the 2023 Act |

### Netiquette — good online behaviour

| Rule / term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Netiquette** | the code of polite, responsible behaviour on the internet ("net etiquette") |
| **Typing in ALL CAPITALS** | reads as SHOUTING — avoid it |
| **Flaming** | posting hostile, insulting messages |
| **Trolling** | deliberately provoking others online to start fights |
| **Spamming** | sending unwanted bulk messages |
| **Respect privacy and copyright** | do not share others' personal data or copy content without credit |
| **Verify before forwarding** | check facts to stop fake news and misinformation |

## Don't confuse
- **Internet** (the network, from ARPANET 1969) ≠ **World Wide Web** (pages on top of it, Berners-Lee 1989).
- **IPv4 = 32-bit; IPv6 = 128-bit.** **HTTP** is plain; **HTTPS** is encrypted.
- **Telecommunications Act 2023** replaced the **Telegraph Act 1885**; the **IT Act 2000** is a different law (cyber offences).
- **Flaming** = insulting; **trolling** = provoking on purpose; **spamming** = bulk unwanted messages.

**Remember it:** "ARPA '69, Web '89, India '95, 5G '22."

**TL;DR**
- ARPANET 1969 → internet; WWW by Tim Berners-Lee at CERN, 1989; VSNL brought the internet to India on 15 August 1995.
- IPv6 = 128-bit; DNS turns names into IP addresses; optical fibre uses total internal reflection.
- 1G analogue → 2G digital/SMS → 3G data → 4G LTE all-IP → 5G low latency.
- Telecom Act 2023 replaced the Telegraph Act 1885; Sanchar Saathi blocks stolen phones.
- Netiquette: no ALL CAPS, no flaming, trolling or spam; respect privacy; verify before forwarding.
keyPoints: ARPANET (1969) — US defence network that grew into the internet.
World Wide Web — created by Tim Berners-Lee at CERN in 1989.
Netiquette — the code of polite, responsible behaviour on the internet ("net etiquette").
Typing in ALL CAPITALS — reads as SHOUTING — avoid it.

items.title: Cyber Threats & Defences — the Glossary
items.body:
## Know your attacker, know your shield

**In one line:** malware comes in families (virus, worm, Trojan, spyware, ransomware), social-engineering tricks come in flavours (phishing by e-mail, vishing by voice, smishing by SMS), and defences are layered (firewall, encryption, two-factor authentication, patching).

**Why it is asked:** "a worm differs from a virus because…", "vishing is…", "WannaCry was a…", "Stuxnet targeted…", "what is a zero-day?" and "digital arrest" scams are frequent statement and match items.

**The story**

A **virus** attaches itself to a file and spreads when that file is run; a **worm** copies itself across networks on its own; a **Trojan horse** pretends to be useful software. **Spyware** and **keyloggers** secretly record what you do; a **rootkit** hides deep in the system. **WannaCry (2017)** was a global **ransomware** attack, and **Stuxnet (2010)** was a worm that damaged **Iran's uranium centrifuges** — the first well-known cyber weapon. A **zero-day** is a flaw that attackers exploit before the maker has a fix.

Fraudsters also attack people, not machines — **social engineering**. In India the fast-growing **"digital arrest" scam** has fraudsters posing as police or customs officers on video calls to frighten victims into paying. Defences: a **firewall** filters network traffic, **encryption** scrambles data so only the key-holder can read it, **two-factor authentication (2FA)** adds a second proof such as an OTP, and **ethical (white-hat) hackers** test systems legally.

### Malware and attacks

| Threat | What it is |
|---|---|
| **Virus** | attaches to a host file and spreads when the file is run |
| **Worm** | self-replicates across networks without a host file |
| **Trojan horse** | malware disguised as useful software |
| **Spyware / keylogger** | secretly records activity or keystrokes |
| **Rootkit** | hides deep in the operating system to keep control |
| **Botnet** | network of infected "zombie" computers run by an attacker, often used for DDoS |
| **Zero-day** | a flaw exploited before the vendor has released a fix |
| **WannaCry (2017)** | worldwide ransomware attack on Windows computers |
| **Stuxnet (2010)** | worm that sabotaged Iran's uranium-enrichment centrifuges |
| **Cryptojacking** | secretly using a victim's computer to mine cryptocurrency |
| **SQL injection** | malicious code typed into a website form to read its database |

### Social-engineering frauds

| Fraud | Method |
|---|---|
| **Spear phishing** | phishing aimed at one specific person or organisation |
| **Whaling** | phishing aimed at top executives |
| **Vishing** | voice phishing over phone calls |
| **Smishing** | phishing by SMS text messages |
| **Pharming** | redirecting users from a real website to a fake one |
| **Quishing** | phishing through malicious QR codes |
| **SIM-swap fraud** | getting a duplicate SIM to receive the victim's OTPs |
| **Juice jacking** | stealing data through infected public USB charging points |
| **"Digital arrest" scam** | fraudsters pose as police or officials on video calls and extort money |
| **Deepfake** | AI-generated fake video or voice of a real person |

### Defences

| Defence | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Firewall** | filters incoming and outgoing network traffic by rules |
| **Encryption** | scrambles data so only the key-holder can read it |
| **Two-factor authentication (2FA)** | adds a second proof such as an OTP to the password |
| **VPN (Virtual Private Network)** | encrypted tunnel over the public internet |
| **Ethical (white-hat) hacking** | authorised testing to find weaknesses |
| **Honeypot** | decoy system that lures and studies attackers |
| **CAPTCHA** | test that tells humans from bots |
| **Dark web** | hidden part of the internet reached through special software such as Tor |

## Don't confuse
- **Virus needs a host file; worm spreads by itself; Trojan pretends to be useful.**
- **Phishing = e-mail; vishing = voice; smishing = SMS; quishing = QR code; pharming = fake website redirect.**
- **Ransomware** locks your data for money (WannaCry); **Stuxnet** physically sabotaged machines.
- **Firewall** filters traffic; **antivirus** removes malware; **encryption** protects the data itself.

**Remember it:** "V for voice, S for SMS, Q for QR."

**TL;DR**
- Virus (host), worm (self-spreading), Trojan (disguise), spyware, rootkit, botnet, zero-day.
- WannaCry 2017 = ransomware; Stuxnet 2010 = worm against Iran's centrifuges.
- Vishing, smishing, quishing, SIM-swap, juice jacking, digital-arrest and deepfake frauds.
- Defences: firewall, encryption, 2FA, VPN, ethical hacking, CAPTCHA.
keyPoints: Virus — attaches to a host file and spreads when the file is run.
Worm — self-replicates across networks without a host file.
Vishing — voice phishing over phone calls.
Smishing — phishing by SMS text messages.
Firewall — filters incoming and outgoing network traffic by rules.
Encryption — scrambles data so only the key-holder can read it.

items.title: Cyber Law in Detail — IT Act Sections, New Laws (2021–2026) & Institutions
items.body:
## The sections and bodies examiners name

**In one line:** the IT Act 2000 lists cyber offences section by section (66 hacking, 66C identity theft, 66D impersonation, 66F cyber terrorism, 67 obscenity, 69A blocking), and a newer layer — IT Rules 2021, the Telecommunications Act 2023, the DPDP Act 2023 and the Online Gaming Act 2025 — governs platforms, telecom, data and gaming.

**Why it is asked:** "cyber terrorism is punished under which section", "website blocking power is in Section…", "the Act has extra-territorial reach under Section 75", "which law bans real-money online games" and "who coordinates national cyber security" are favourite items, and the Mains syllabus names cyber-law **jurisdiction**.

**The story**

The **IT Act 2000** came into force on **17 October 2000** and gave legal status to electronic records and **digital signatures**, issued by Certifying Authorities under the **Controller of Certifying Authorities (CCA)**. **Section 75** gives it **extra-territorial jurisdiction**: it applies to an offence committed outside India if it involves a computer or network located in India. Appeals once went to the Cyber Appellate Tribunal, which was merged into **TDSAT in 2017**.

Newer rules sit on top: the **IT (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021** require platforms to appoint grievance officers and set a three-tier code for digital news and OTT. The **Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Act, 2025** (assent 22 August 2025) **bans real-money online games** while promoting e-sports; its rules were notified in April 2026.

Institutions: **CERT-In** began in **2004**; **NCIIPC** was notified in **2014**; **I4C** was launched in **January 2020**; the **National Cyber Security Coordinator** sits in the **National Security Council Secretariat (PMO)**; and the **Defence Cyber Agency** handles military cyber operations. India has **not joined the Budapest Convention (2001)** on cybercrime; the new **UN Convention against Cybercrime** was adopted in December 2024 and opened for signature in **Hanoi in October 2025**.

### IT Act 2000 — key sections

| Section | Offence / provision |
|---|---|
| **Section 43** | damage to a computer system without permission — civil compensation |
| **Section 65** | tampering with computer source code |
| **Section 66** | computer-related offences such as hacking |
| **Section 66C** | identity theft (misusing passwords, digital signatures) |
| **Section 66D** | cheating by personation using a computer |
| **Section 66E** | violation of privacy — capturing or sharing private images |
| **Section 66F** | cyber terrorism — punishable with up to life imprisonment |
| **Section 67 (67A, 67B)** | publishing obscene, sexually explicit or child sexual abuse material |
| **Section 69A** | power of the Centre to block websites and online content |
| **Section 75** | extra-territorial jurisdiction — offences abroad that involve a computer in India |
| **Commencement** | the IT Act came into force on 17 October 2000 |
| **Controller of Certifying Authorities (CCA)** | licenses the bodies that issue digital signature certificates |
| **Cyber Appellate Tribunal** | merged into TDSAT in 2017 |

### Newer digital laws and rules

| Law / rule | Fact |
|---|---|
| **IT (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021** | grievance officers for platforms; three-tier code for digital news and OTT |
| **Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Act, 2025** | bans real-money online games; promotes e-sports (assent 22 August 2025) |
| **DPDP Act, 2023 — assent** | received Presidential assent on 11 August 2023 |
| **Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023** | lists cyber-crime within "organised crime" (Section 111) |

### Cyber and digital institutions

| Body | Fact |
|---|---|
| **CERT-In** | set up in 2004 |
| **NCIIPC** | notified in January 2014 |
| **I4C** | launched in January 2020 (approved 2018) under the MHA |
| **National Cyber Security Coordinator** | heads cyber-security coordination in the National Security Council Secretariat (PMO) |
| **Defence Cyber Agency** | tri-service agency for military cyber operations |
| **National Informatics Centre (NIC, 1976)** | builds and hosts the government's websites and e-governance systems |
| **C-DAC (1988, Pune)** | built PARAM 8000 (1991), India's first supercomputer |
| **C-DOT (1984)** | telecom R&D centre founded under Sam Pitroda |
| **UIDAI (2009)** | issues the 12-digit Aadhaar number; statutory under the Aadhaar Act 2016 |
| **Budapest Convention (2001)** | Council of Europe cybercrime treaty — India is not a party |
| **UN Convention against Cybercrime** | adopted December 2024; opened for signature in Hanoi, October 2025 |

## Don't confuse
- **66C = identity theft; 66D = cheating by personation; 66E = privacy; 66F = cyber terrorism (life imprisonment).**
- **69 = interception; 69A = blocking; 70A = NCIIPC; 70B = CERT-In; 75 = jurisdiction abroad; 79 = safe harbour.**
- **IT Rules 2021** (platforms) ≠ **DPDP Rules 2025** (personal data) ≠ **Online Gaming Rules 2026** (gaming).
- India is **not** in the Budapest Convention.

**Remember it:** "C-D-E-F: Credentials stolen, Disguise, Exposure, Fear (terror)."

**TL;DR**
- IT Act 2000 (in force 17 Oct 2000): 66 hacking, 66C identity theft, 66D personation, 66F cyber terrorism, 69A blocking, 75 extra-territorial reach.
- IT Rules 2021; Online Gaming Act 2025 bans real-money games; BNS 2023 lists cyber-crime as organised crime.
- CERT-In 2004, NCIIPC 2014, I4C 2020, NCSC in NSCS; NIC 1976, C-DAC 1988, C-DOT 1984, UIDAI 2009.
keyPoints: Section 66 — computer-related offences such as hacking.
Section 66C — identity theft (misusing passwords, digital signatures).
IT (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 — grievance officers for platforms; three-tier code for digital news and OTT.
Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Act, 2025 — bans real-money online games; promotes e-sports (assent 22 August 2025).
CERT-In — set up in 2004.
National Cyber Security Coordinator — heads cyber-security coordination in the National Security Council Secretariat (PMO).

items.title: e-Governance Platform Directory — NeGP to DPI (2006–2026)
items.body:
## Every platform, with its one-line job

**In one line:** India's e-governance moved from the **National e-Governance Plan (2006)** with its Mission Mode Projects, through **Digital India (2015)**, to a full **Digital Public Infrastructure** — with a separate platform for payments, health, education, farming, procurement, grievances and language.

**Why it is asked:** match-the-platform questions ("e-NAM is for…", "SWAYAM is…", "PRAGATI reviews…", "Bhashini does…"), the **2nd ARC's SMART** formula and UPI's global reach are steady Paper-II and Mains material.

**The story**

The **National e-Governance Plan (NeGP, 2006)** organised e-governance as **Mission Mode Projects** (passports, income tax, land records, e-courts and so on); its successor **e-Kranti (NeGP 2.0, 2015)** sits inside Digital India. The **2nd Administrative Reforms Commission (11th report, "Promoting e-Governance — the SMART Way Forward")** defined good e-governance as **SMART — Simple, Moral, Accountable, Responsive and Transparent**. The **JAM trinity** — **Jan Dhan accounts, Aadhaar and Mobile** — is the base for **Direct Benefit Transfer**. UPI has grown from **16 billion transactions a month (2024-25)** to about **20 billion a month (August 2025)** and is accepted in countries such as **Singapore, the UAE, France, Bhutan, Nepal, Sri Lanka and Mauritius**. The RBI's **digital rupee (e₹)** — a central bank digital currency — has been piloted since **December 2022** for retail use.

### National e-governance platforms

| Platform | Job |
|---|---|
| **NeGP (2006)** | National e-Governance Plan of Mission Mode Projects |
| **2nd ARC — SMART governance** | Simple, Moral, Accountable, Responsive, Transparent |
| **JAM trinity** | Jan Dhan accounts + Aadhaar + Mobile — the base for Direct Benefit Transfer |
| **BHIM (2016)** | NPCI's UPI app |
| **e-RUPI (2021)** | purpose-specific prepaid digital voucher on UPI |
| **Digital rupee (e₹)** | RBI's central bank digital currency — retail pilot since December 2022 |
| **GeM (2016)** | Government e-Marketplace for public procurement |
| **e-NAM (2016)** | online national market for farm produce linking mandis |
| **Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (2021)** | 14-digit ABHA health ID and digital health records |
| **eSanjeevani** | national telemedicine service |
| **SWAYAM (2017)** | free online courses (MOOCs) |
| **DIKSHA (2017)** | digital learning platform for school teachers and students |
| **MyGov (2014)** | citizen-participation platform for ideas and feedback |
| **PRAGATI (2015)** | the Prime Minister's video-conference platform to review projects and grievances |
| **CPGRAMS** | online public-grievance redress system of the Centre |
| **Bhashini (2022)** | AI platform for translation across Indian languages |
| **e-Courts Mission Mode Project** | digitises court records and allows e-filing and virtual hearings |
| **UPI abroad** | accepted in Singapore, the UAE, France, Bhutan, Nepal, Sri Lanka and Mauritius |
| **UPI volume (August 2025)** | about 20 billion transactions in a single month |

## Don't confuse
- **NeGP (2006)** is the old plan of Mission Mode Projects; **e-Kranti (2015)** is NeGP 2.0 within Digital India.
- **e-RUPI** is a **voucher** on UPI; the **digital rupee (e₹)** is the RBI's **currency**.
- **SWAYAM = MOOCs for learners; DIKSHA = school teachers; e-NAM = farm markets; GeM = government buying.**
- **ABHA = 14-digit health ID; Aadhaar = 12-digit identity number.**

**Remember it:** SMART = "Simple Moral Accountable Responsive Transparent."

**TL;DR**
- NeGP 2006 → e-Kranti 2015; 2nd ARC: SMART governance; JAM trinity powers DBT.
- Payments: UPI (about 20 billion a month by Aug 2025, used abroad), BHIM, e-RUPI, digital rupee (pilot Dec 2022).
- GeM, e-NAM, ABDM/ABHA, eSanjeevani, SWAYAM, DIKSHA, MyGov, PRAGATI, CPGRAMS, Bhashini, e-Courts.
keyPoints: NeGP (2006) — National e-Governance Plan of Mission Mode Projects.
2nd ARC — SMART governance — Simple, Moral, Accountable, Responsive, Transparent.

items.title: Frontier Technologies — AI, IoT, Quantum, Chips & Supercomputers (Terms and Indian Milestones)
items.body:
## The vocabulary of the digital frontier

**In one line:** AI learns from data (machine learning, deep learning, large language models), IoT connects everyday objects, quantum computers use qubits in superposition and entanglement, and India is building its own chips, supercomputers and AI models.

**Why it is asked:** "who coined the term AI", "what is the Turing test", "what is quantum entanglement", "AIRAWAT is…", "India's first indigenous space-grade microprocessor" and "where was the 2026 AI summit" are current and conceptual items.

**The story**

**John McCarthy** coined the term **"artificial intelligence" (Dartmouth, 1956)**, and **Alan Turing (1950)** proposed the **Turing test** of whether a machine can pass for a human. **Machine learning** lets computers learn patterns from data; **deep learning** uses many-layered **neural networks**; **generative AI** and **large language models (LLMs)** create text, images and code. **IoT (Internet of Things)**, a term coined by **Kevin Ashton (1999)**, links sensors and devices; **edge computing** processes data near where it is produced. A **qubit** can be 0 and 1 at once (**superposition**), and linked qubits share states (**entanglement**). India hosted the **AI Impact Summit at Bharat Mandapam, New Delhi (February 2026)** — the first in the series held in the Global South. In chips, ISRO and the **Semi-Conductor Laboratory (Mohali)** produced **Vikram 3201** (September 2025), India's first fully indigenous **32-bit space-grade microprocessor**.

### AI, data and computing terms

| Term | Meaning / fact |
|---|---|
| **John McCarthy** | coined "artificial intelligence" at the Dartmouth conference, 1956 |
| **Turing test (1950)** | Alan Turing's test of whether a machine's replies can pass for a human's |
| **Machine learning** | computers learn patterns from data instead of fixed rules |
| **Deep learning** | machine learning with many-layered neural networks |
| **Large language model (LLM)** | generative AI trained on huge text to produce human-like language (e.g. ChatGPT) |
| **Artificial general intelligence (AGI)** | hypothetical AI matching humans across all tasks (today's AI is narrow) |
| **Internet of Things (IoT)** | everyday devices with sensors connected to the internet — term coined by Kevin Ashton (1999) |
| **Edge computing** | processing data near its source instead of a distant cloud |
| **Big data** | data sets defined by volume, velocity and variety |
| **Digital twin** | live virtual copy of a physical object or system |
| **AR vs VR** | augmented reality overlays digital objects on the real world; virtual reality replaces it entirely |
| **3D printing** | additive manufacturing — building an object layer by layer |

### Quantum, chips, supercomputers and AI in India

| Item | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Superposition** | a qubit can be 0 and 1 at the same time |
| **Entanglement** | linked qubits share one state even when far apart |
| **Quantum supremacy (2019)** | Google's Sycamore processor claimed a task no classical computer could do in practical time |
| **Quantum key distribution (QKD)** | sharing encryption keys whose secrecy is guaranteed by physics |
| **Moore's law** | transistors on a chip roughly double every two years |
| **Vikram 3201 (September 2025)** | India's first fully indigenous 32-bit space-grade microprocessor — ISRO and SCL Mohali |
| **Semi-Conductor Laboratory (SCL)** | government chip fab at Mohali, Punjab |
| **Micron (Sanand, Gujarat)** | US firm's chip assembly and test (ATMP) unit |
| **Tata–PSMC (Dholera, Gujarat)** | India's first commercial semiconductor fab, with Taiwan's PSMC |
| **India Semiconductor Mission** | launched December 2021 under MeitY |
| **AIRAWAT** | India's AI supercomputer at C-DAC Pune |
| **Pratyush and Mihir; Arka and Arunika** | weather-and-climate supercomputers at IITM Pune and NCMRWF Noida |
| **BharatGen (2024)** | government-funded multilingual, multimodal Indian AI model initiative |
| **India AI Impact Summit (February 2026)** | held at Bharat Mandapam, New Delhi — first in the series hosted by a Global South country |
| **Drone Rules 2021** | liberalised drone flying with green, yellow and red airspace zones |
| **Amaravati Quantum Valley MoU (4 May 2025)** | AP signed with IBM, TCS and L&T to install a 156-qubit IBM Quantum System Two |

## Don't confuse
- **AI (the field) ⊃ machine learning ⊃ deep learning.** Today's AI is **narrow**; AGI is still hypothetical.
- **Superposition** = one qubit in two states; **entanglement** = two qubits linked.
- **AIRAWAT = AI supercomputer; PARAM Rudra = National Supercomputing Mission; Pratyush/Mihir/Arka/Arunika = weather.**
- **Vikram 3201** is a **microprocessor**; **Vikram-S** is a private **rocket** (Skyroot).
- **AR adds to reality; VR replaces it.**

**Remember it:** "McCarthy named it (1956), Turing tested it (1950), Ashton connected it (IoT 1999)."

**TL;DR**
- AI term: McCarthy 1956; Turing test 1950; ML → deep learning → LLMs.
- IoT (Ashton 1999), edge computing, big data (volume, velocity, variety), digital twin, AR/VR, 3D printing.
- Qubit superposition and entanglement; QKD; Google Sycamore 2019.
- Chips: ISM (Dec 2021), Tata–PSMC Dholera fab, Micron Sanand, SCL Mohali, Vikram 3201 (Sept 2025).
- AIRAWAT AI supercomputer; AI Impact Summit, Bharat Mandapam, February 2026.
keyPoints: John McCarthy — coined "artificial intelligence" at the Dartmouth conference, 1956.
Turing test (1950) — Alan Turing's test of whether a machine's replies can pass for a human's.
Superposition — a qubit can be 0 and 1 at the same time.
Entanglement — linked qubits share one state even when far apart.

items.title: For Mains — ICT, e-Governance & Cyber Security
items.body:
## In one line
How to turn the ICT/e-governance/cyber facts into Mains answers for Paper-V (M5-2: ICT, e-governance, cyber crime & security policy, IT policy in AP & India) and the Paper-III Cyber-Law clause (M3-15d).

## The dimensions Mains asks

| Dimension | What to write |
|---|---|
| Significance of ICT | Enabler of governance, financial inclusion, service delivery; India Stack / DPI model |
| e-governance | Digital India, G2C/G2B/G2G/G2E; UMANG, DigiLocker, UPI; AP's RTGS, Mana Mitra |
| Cyber crime & security | Rising threats (phishing, ransomware, deepfakes); CERT-In, NCIIPC, I4C; CFCFRMS |
| Legal framework | IT Act 2000 (66A struck down), DPDP Act 2023 & Rules 2025, National Cyber Security Policy 2013 |
| Challenges | Digital divide, data privacy, consent fatigue, cyber-skilling gap, AI-deepfake fraud |
| Way forward | Updated cyber strategy, privacy-by-design, last-mile access, public-private cooperation |

## Data points to quote
- UPI = world's largest real-time retail payment system (16 billion+ monthly, 2024-25).
- DPDP Act 2023 (penalty up to ₹250 crore) + DPDP Rules 2025; Section 66A struck down (Shreya Singhal, 2015).
- CERT-In 2022 directions (6-hour reporting); I4C + 1930 helpline + CFCFRMS.
- IndiaAI Mission (2024, ₹10,372 cr); National Quantum Mission (2023, ₹6,003 cr).

## AP angle
AP leads in tech-governance: **Real Time Governance Centre**, **e-Pragati**, **Mana Mitra** (WhatsApp G2C), **AP FiberNet**, and frontier bets like the **Amaravati Quantum Valley** (IBM-TCS, 156-qubit) and the **Google 1 GW AI data-centre hub at Visakhapatnam**.

## Use in answers
- **Example:** cite UPI and DBT as proof that DPI deepens inclusion and cuts leakage.
- **Quote:** frame the trade-off as "digital empowerment vs digital divide and privacy".
- **Diagram idea:** a DPI pyramid (identity → payments → data → services) or a cyber-defence layering (CERT-In / NCIIPC / I4C).

## TL;DR
- Structure: significance → e-governance → cyber security → law → challenges → way forward, with an AP paragraph.
- Lead with the India Stack/UPI success and balance it with privacy and digital-divide concerns.
- For cyber-law questions (M3-15d), centre the IT Act 2000, DPDP 2023/Rules 2025 and the institutional trio.
